Skip to content
Back
Capture quality

Experimental (off)

Turn on experimental metrics in Profile to see this.

This session has a value. Experimental: we're still checking this method, so treat it as a rough guide. It never feeds coaching.

What it is

Can I trust this session's numbers?

How well we could see this session: Good, Fair or Limited.

How we measure it
We check framing, light, steadiness, frame rate and how clearly we saw the ball and your body on each serve.
How sure we are

Tested on simulated serves, but those tests can't settle it yet, so it stays experimental.

On simulated clips, the view check caught all 5 clips filmed from in front instead of the side, and the tilt check turned down all 5 clips with the phone tipped up. The other checks are only tested one by one.

Known limits
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.
More in How we measure

own-metric-toss-height-default75-s1.text:
Skip to content
Back
Toss height

Needs more serves

Record at least 8 serves from one side.

Not available from this footage.

What it is

How high do I toss?

How high your toss peaks, as a multiple of your height.

How we measure it
We follow the ball from your toss hand, fit its path, and find the top of its flight.
We measure the peak above the court using your height as the scale.
Peaks above the picture are estimated from the curve of the ball and marked "Peak estimated".
What it needs
30 fps or more
Yes
Toss peak seen
Not checked
Feet in the picture
Not checked
Standing height in the picture
Not checked
Phone tilt known
No

For the session on Mon 28 Sep.

How sure we are

Checked on simulated serves in daylight. Not yet checked on real courts.

Not yet checked under court lights, so at night it shows as experimental.

At the recommended set-ups (11 simulated serves filmed 7 to 9 m away), the typical error was about 1% of your height (about 2 cm for you), and 1 in 20 serves was off by about 2.5% of your height (about 5 cm for you) or more.

Our stated range held the true value on 11 of 11 of those serves.

Our pass mark is a typical error within 2.5% of your height, and 1 in 20 serves within 5%. It passed.

Filming closer than about 6 m made heights read low, so those serves are marked experimental. A tilted phone, or one whose tilt we could not read, does the same.

Test details
Known limits
From the side, a toss nearer the camera than your body reads a little high, and a little sideways wobble adds a few centimetres to the spread. A view from behind separates the two.
Heights and distances depend on your entered height, so the whole set could sit a few centimetres high or low. Comparisons with your own serves are sharper than the absolute numbers.
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.
More in How we measure

Skip to content

Leg drive (hip rise)

Needs more serves

Record at least 8 serves from one side.

Not available from this footage.

What it is

Am I using my legs?

How far your hips rise from their lowest point to contact, as a share of your height. It describes how you use your legs, compared with your own serves.

How we measure it
We track the middle of your hips through the serve.
We find their lowest point after the toss.
We measure how far they rise by contact, as a share of your height.
What it needs
Side view
Yes
30 fps or more
Yes
Toss release found
Not checked
Contact found
Not checked
Standing height in the picture
Not checked
Hips visible
Not checked

For the session on Mon 28 Sep.

How sure we are

Checked on simulated serves in daylight, on limited evidence so far. Not yet checked on real courts.

Not yet checked under court lights, so at night it shows as experimental.

At the recommended set-ups (11 simulated serves filmed 7 to 9 m away), the typical error was about 2.5% of your height, and 1 in 20 serves was off by about 3% of your height or more.

Our stated range held the true value on 11 of 11 of those serves.

Our pass mark is a typical error within 2% of your height. It hasn't passed yet.

Most of the error is a steady offset: the tracker reads your hip rise a little low on every serve, so comparisons with your own serves aren't affected.

Test details
Known limits
From the side your knees point at the camera at the top of the swing, so we describe your legs by hip rise and hip drop instead of a knee angle. A knee-bend band needs the view from behind.
Body tracking from phone video is noisier than lab systems, and left and right can swap. We assign sides from the shape of the serve.
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.
Compared with your own serves

We compare this only with your own usual serves. Published trunk angles and professional leg values measure different things, so we don't show them.

More in How we measure

Estimate: worked out from your video and your height, so it has a margin of error.

What it is

How many serves did I hit?

How many serves we found in the video.

How we measure it
We find each serve from your toss arm, the ball above your head and the hit.
What it needs
30 fps or more
Yes

For the session on Mon 28 Sep.

How sure we are

Checked on simulated serves in daylight, on limited evidence so far. Not yet checked on real courts.

Not yet checked under court lights, so at night it shows as experimental.

At the recommended set-ups (11 simulated serves filmed 7 to 9 m away), every serve was found, with no extras, and the same across 95 simulated side-view clips.

Our pass mark is at least 99 of 100 serves found, with no extras. It passed.

Run through the full app, from video to report, two longer simulated sessions of 8 and 16 serves were harder: it found every serve but was unsure of 3 and left them out, so the count read 1 or 2 short. Those serves stay in your list, marked as excluded, and you can include them again.

Test details
Known limits
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.

own-metric-spin-default75-s1.text:
Skip to content
Back
Spin

Not measurable by phone

Spin needs cameras shooting about 1,000 frames a second or a radar tracker; phone video can't measure it. Log the serve type you meant instead.

Never measured, whatever the footage.

What it is

How much spin did I use?

How much spin you put on the ball.

How we measure it
A phone video cannot see the ball spinning: it is too small and too blurred. We never estimate it.
How sure we are

Phone video can't see spin, so there is nothing to check and it is never shown as a number.

Known limits
From the side, speed needs 120 fps or more, your height and where you aimed. From behind it needs the court corners tapped and a bounce in the video. The hit sound never gives speed. Spin is never available.
More in How we measure

What it is

Can I trust this session's numbers?

How well we could see this session: Good, Fair or Limited.

How we measure it
We check framing, light, steadiness, frame rate and how clearly we saw the ball and your body on each serve.
How sure we are

Tested on simulated serves, but those tests can't settle it yet, so it stays experimental.

On simulated clips, the view check caught all 5 clips filmed from in front instead of the side, and the tilt check turned down all 5 clips with the phone tipped up. The other checks are only tested one by one.

Toss height

Experimental (off)

Turn on experimental metrics in Profile to see this.

This session has a value. Experimental: we're still checking this method, so treat it as a rough guide. It never feeds coaching.

What it is

How high do I toss?

How high your toss peaks, as a multiple of your height.

How we measure it
We follow the ball from your toss hand, fit its path, and find the top of its flight.
We measure the peak above the court using your height as the scale.
Peaks above the picture are estimated from the curve of the ball and marked "Peak estimated".
What it needs
30 fps or more
Yes
Toss peak seen
Yes
Feet in the picture
Yes
Standing height in the picture
Yes
Phone tilt known
No

For the session on Mon 28 Sep.

How sure we are

Checked on simulated serves in daylight. Not yet checked on real courts.

Not yet checked under court lights, so at night it shows as experimental.

At the recommended set-ups (11 simulated serves filmed 7 to 9 m away), the typical error was about 1% of your height (about 2 cm for you), and 1 in 20 serves was off by about 2.5% of your height (about 5 cm for you) or more.

Our stated range held the true value on 11 of 11 of those serves.

Our pass mark is a typical error within 2.5% of your height, and 1 in 20 serves within 5%. It passed.

Filming closer than about 6 m made heights read low, so those serves are marked experimental. A tilted phone, or one whose tilt we could not read, does the same.

Test details
Known limits
From the side, a toss nearer the camera than your body reads a little high, and a little sideways wobble adds a few centimetres to the spread. A view from behind separates the two.
Heights and distances depend on your entered height, so the whole set could sit a few centimetres high or low. Comparisons with your own serves are sharper than the absolute numbers.
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.

At the recommended set-ups (11 simulated serves filmed 7 to 9 m away), the typical error was about 2.5% of your height, and 1 in 20 serves was off by about 3% of your height or more.

Our stated range held the true value on 11 of 11 of those serves.

Test details
Known limits
From the side your knees point at the camera at the top of the swing, so we describe your legs by hip rise and hip drop instead of a knee angle. A knee-bend band needs the view from behind.
Body tracking from phone video is noisier than lab systems, and left and right can swap. We assign sides from the shape of the serve.
Every check so far used computer-generated serves: one simulated player on a rendered court, filmed by our own model of a phone camera. Real players, phones, courts and court lights may do worse.
Compared with your own serves

We compare this only with your own usual serves. Published trunk angles and professional leg values measure different things, so we don't show them.

Spin

Not measurable by phone

Spin needs cameras shooting about 1,000 frames a second or a radar tracker; phone video can't measure it. Log the serve type you meant instead.

Never measured, whatever the footage.

What it is

How much spin did I use?

How much spin you put on the ball.

How we measure it
A phone video cannot see the ball spinning: it is too small and too blurred. We never estimate it.
How sure we are

Phone video can't see spin, so there is nothing to check and it is never shown as a number.

Known limits
From the side, speed needs 120 fps or more, your height and where you aimed. From behind it needs the court corners tapped and a bounce in the video. The hit sound never gives speed. Spin is never available.
More in How we measure
